enquiry: Our dairy process includes a relatively clear whey stream before a concentration stage. We want to investigate whether spectroscopy can track protein concentration as the stream changes, with laboratory results used as the reference. The stream can become more turbid under some operating conditions. We need a first measurement concept that handles this change rather than assuming the liquid always remains clear.

recommendations.rationale: NIR transmission/transflection is the standard in-line technique for clear dairy liquids and whey is named as a suitable sample in the dairy example. The nominal NIR range is 780-2500 nm; the usable range depends on the instrument, fiber and probe selected.

citations.quote: Transmission is the preferred method for transparent or semi-transparent liquids, such as skim milk, whey, or permeate.
NIR spectra (780-2500 nm) contain predominantly overtones and component bands of fundamental vibrations

recommendations.rationale: Raman tolerates water and scattering better than absorption methods, making it a useful comparison if turbidity degrades the NIR signal. Weak Raman signals and possible fluorescence background must be checked on real whey samples.

citations.quote: Raman is particularly well-suited for aqueous environments, as it exhibits low absorbance for water molecules compared to infrared methods.

recommendations.rationale: If turbidity or overlapping whey components limit the single methods, a combined NIR+Raman option is the next hypothesis, to be tested against the best single method. Any fusion gain is a hypothesis and requires synchronised, same-spot measurement.
recommendations.conditions: Only if the feasibility trial shows that neither NIR nor Raman alone meets the required accuracy across the turbidity range.

citations.quote: The analysis of such systems may require a combination of two or even more spectral methods.

recommendations.rationale: NIR diffuse reflection is designated for opaque, highly concentrated dairy products and is sensitive to surface characteristics, so it does not fit a relatively clear liquid stream and was screened out for this sample type.

citations.quote: NIR Reflection is primarily used for opaque or highly concentrated dairy products, such as yogurt, butter, or whole milk concentrates.

measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: NIR transmission or transflection fiber probe with a controlled optical pathlength (typically 1-10 mm in the dairy example); a transflection probe is the candidate that may cover both clear and turbid states.
measurement_concept.location: In-line probe in the whey stream upstream of the concentration stage, at a point that is representative across the turbidity variation.
measurement_concept.fiber_link: Vis-NIR silica fibers are compatible with the NIR range; the achievable cable length depends on the selected fiber and installation and must be confirmed with AFS.

citations.quote: the precise control of the optical pathlength (usually 1 - 10 mm); if the pathlength is too wide, the signal is lost to absorption; if too narrow, the sample represents a negligible volume.

citations.quote: the method is sensitive to the surface characteristics and fat globule size.

risks.risk: Overlapping NIR bands of lactose, fat and protein in whey mean the calibration quality depends heavily on the number and representativeness of reference samples.

citations.quote: The broad absorption bands observed in this region overlap, suggesting the use of chemometrics for quantitative and qualitative analysis of spectral data.

solution_options.fusion_note: Low-level data fusion: NIR and Raman spectra synchronised to a common time step and merged into one augmented matrix, with per-method calibration blocks. Both probes must sample the same material at the same point in the stream. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs, otherwise the second instrument should be dropped.

citations.quote: By combining Raman and NIR, these models can predict API potency or coating thickness with higher accuracy and robustness than single-method models.

assessment.chemometrics_note: A PLS calibration for protein will need representative samples spanning the full turbidity and composition range; scatter correction (e.g. MSC or SNV) is standard practice for scattering dairy samples, and the model must be validated on held-out production runs.
assessment.realtime_tracking_note: The goal is continuous in-line tracking of protein as the stream changes; NIR diode-array instruments allow fast acquisition, and the calibration must remain valid across the turbidity transients, which is exactly what the trial must demonstrate.
assessment.future_direction: If the feasibility trial succeeds, a customized in-line system at the measurement point with automated data transfer for process control is a later extension.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the turbidity change proves severe or the protein range is very low, the Raman comparison or the NIR+Raman combination would move up; if the lab reference method or accuracy requirement differs from what is assumed, the whole plan needs revisiting.
proposal.next_step: Run a lab feasibility trial on representative whey samples spanning the turbidity range, with your laboratory protein results as reference.

assessment.brief_answer: Test NIR transmission/transflection first: it is the standard in-line technique for clear dairy streams such as whey, and a transflection probe may in some cases also cover the turbid states. Raman is the comparison method because it tolerates water and scattering. Open points: the protein range, the cause and degree of turbidity, the lab reference method, and the installation point. A lab feasibility trial on representative samples with your lab results as reference is the proposed next step.

recommendations.rationale: Raman tolerates water and scattering better than absorption methods, making it a useful comparison if turbidity degrades the NIR signal. Weak Raman signals and possible fluorescence background must be checked on real whey samples.

assessment.chemometrics_note: A PLS calibration for protein will need representative samples spanning the full turbidity and composition range; scatter correction (e.g. MSC or SNV) is standard practice for scattering dairy samples, and the model must be validated on held-out production runs.
assessment.realtime_tracking_note: The goal is continuous in-line tracking of protein as the stream changes; NIR diode-array instruments allow fast acquisition, and the calibration must remain valid across the turbidity transients, which is exactly what the trial must demonstrate.
assessment.future_direction: If the feasibility trial succeeds, a customized in-line system at the measurement point with automated data transfer for process control is a later extension.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the turbidity change proves severe or the protein range is very low, the Raman comparison or the NIR+Raman combination would move up; if the lab reference method or accuracy requirement differs from what is assumed, the whole plan needs revisiting.
proposal.next_step: Run a lab feasibility trial on representative whey samples spanning the turbidity range, with your laboratory protein results as reference.

assessment.brief_answer: Test NIR transmission/transflection first: it is the standard in-line technique for clear dairy streams such as whey, and a transflection probe may in some cases also cover the turbid states. Raman is the comparison method because it tolerates water and scattering. Open points: the protein range, the cause and degree of turbidity, the lab reference method, and the installation point. A lab feasibility trial on representative samples with your lab results as reference is the proposed next step.

items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest way to combine inputs, by rearranging variables from different sources into a single new data matrix placed one after the other.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the proposed O3 concept of merging synchronised NIR and Raman spectra into one augmented matrix; the assessment can check that the implementation follows this simple concatenation approach with per-method calibration blocks.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The review is general and not dairy- or whey-specific; it describes the method concept, not measured performance for protein in turbid whey.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E02 ¶31

items.finding: The review states that before fusing data from multiple sources, the contribution of each dataset and its complementarity must be evaluated.
items.how_it_applies: This justifies the acceptance rule that the fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs, and that the second instrument should be dropped if it adds no contribution.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: It is a methodological recommendation from a review, not a demonstrated result for NIR/Raman fusion on whey; actual benefit must be tested on this stream.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
citation.label: E02 ¶82

items.finding: The review notes that in some situations, including a Raman and FT-IR food analytical study, instrument complementarity alone was not sufficient to improve predictive performance for several quality attributes.
items.how_it_applies: This is a reason to test, on held-out runs, whether adding Raman to NIR actually improves protein prediction in whey rather than assuming the second instrument helps.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study is food analysis with Raman/FT-IR, not in-line NIR/Raman on a whey process, so the outcome may differ for this matrix and setup.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36

items.finding: In an FT-IR/Raman extraction study, concentration, ionic strength and temperature were deliberately varied to obtain a robust model.
items.how_it_applies: This suggests building the whey calibration with temperature deliberately varied (and recorded) so temperature effects are represented, and using the temperature sensor readings to check whether the model stays robust across the operating range.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The result comes from a lithium-recycling liquid-liquid extraction system, not a dairy whey stream, and concerns model design rather than a specific temperature sensor specification.

citation.quote: The concentrations of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid as well as the ionic strength and temperature were varied to obtain a robust model.
citation.label: E01 ¶19

items.finding: The study reports that in-line maintenance burdens such as calibration and sensor drift or aging can be addressed by checking the baseline in each cycle of pure component phases and monitoring drift so one can react.
items.how_it_applies: For the whey concept, a routine baseline/drift check (with temperature logged alongside) can be planned as part of the auxiliary-sensor and maintenance regime to detect drift that might otherwise be mistaken for composition changes.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This practice is described for a reactive extraction process with recurring pure-component phases, which a continuous whey stream may not have; transfer of the exact check cycle is uncertain.

citation.quote: Potential typical drawbacks of any in-line method are maintenance efforts like calibration, and actions to sensor drift and aging could be easily overcome by checking the baseline in each cycle of pure component phases of process operation and monitoring any drift in order to be able to react.
citation.label: E01 ¶72
